texto:
A creative management platform (CMP) is software that lets an advertiser, agency or publisher build advertising creative once and then produce, adapt, distribute and measure many versions of it. A single master design, fed with product data, copy and audience rules, becomes hundreds or thousands of sized and localised ads, each exported as a file or tag that a media platform can serve. The category exists because demand for variants outran the people who make them. Celtra, one of the companies that popularised the label, called this the "Content Gap": the distance between the volume of creative that campaigns require and the resources available to produce it. Victor Wong of Thunder framed it differently in April 2017, telling ExchangeWire that a CMP "makes creative work doable by non-creative professionals", in the way a data management platform had opened audience data to non-specialists.
From template to tag
The workflow inside a CMP runs in five broad steps, although vendors package them differently.
Templating comes first. A designer builds a master creative, often in HTML5 for display or as a layered video project, and marks which elements may change: headline, price, image, background, call to action, legal copy. Locked elements, such as the logo position or brand typeface, enforce guidelines automatically. Clinch's Creative Template Catalog, released on February 24, 2026, organises such templates by vertical and key performance indicator.
Versioning fills the variable slots. Inputs usually arrive as a spreadsheet, a product feed or an asset library. A retailer running 40 products across 12 sizes in five languages needs 2,400 assets before any audience variation is added; a CMP generates them in a batch and resizes layouts to each format. Smartly said its clients produce more than 150 million creative variants a month.
Review routes the output through approval. Comment threads, version histories and role permissions replace email chains between brand, agency and legal teams.
Activation sends each finished unit to where it will run. For walled gardens such as Meta, TikTok or Snap, the CMP typically pushes assets through the platform's application programming interface (API). For the open web, it exports a JavaScript or iframe tag for display, or a Video Ad Serving Template (VAST) tag for video, which an ad operations team loads into a demand-side platform (DSP) or ad server. Certification matters here: Celtra announced on April 17, 2025 that tags built in its platform were certified for Amazon DSP, removing manual reformatting. Once in the auction, the creative is identified like any other: in OpenRTB the bid response carries the markup in the adm field and an identifier in crid.
Measurement closes the loop. Because each variant carries metadata about its components, a CMP can report performance by element rather than by ad, showing whether a red background or a price-led headline drove clicks. Innovid's Auto Classification, announced on August 25, 2025, uses image recognition to tag those elements automatically.
Who runs it, and where it sits
On the buy side, operators range from in-house brand studios and agency production hubs to performance teams that need fresh variants weekly. On the sell side, publishers use CMPs to build custom formats for sponsors. The platform sits between design tools and buying tools: upstream of the DSP, the social ad manager and the ad server, downstream of the creative brief.
The boundary with the ad server is the most contested line in the category. Some vendors only produce and export creative, leaving delivery to Google's Campaign Manager 360 or another server. Others serve the ads themselves and add real-time decisioning. When Forrester evaluated what it called creative advertising technologies in Q4 2020, it scored separately for ad building and assembly, ad serving, decisioning, workflow and identity. Its leaders were Innovid, Jivox, Clinch and Flashtalking, most of which also served ads; Celtra, primarily a production tool, was placed as a contender.
From rich media to creative automation
The roots lie in the rich media vendors of the 2000s, which built expandable and interactive formats and served them, and in early dynamic creative tools that assembled display ads from product feeds. Celtra, founded by Miha Mikek, Matevz Klanjsek and Maja Mikek, was among the companies that moved the emphasis from formats to production at scale. By 2017 "creative management platform" had become a recognised label, promoted by Thunder and Celtra and tied, in Wong's words, to "programmatic's rise". He argued at the time that more than 90% of programmatic campaigns paying for data targeting had not built creative specific to that data.
Consolidation followed. Sizmek, which combined ad serving with dynamic creative optimisation (DCO), filed for Chapter 11 protection in the US in March 2019; Amazon bought its ad server and DCO business, a deal reported on June 3, 2019. Mediaocean announced on July 13, 2021 that it would acquire Flashtalking, an independent ad server with personalisation tools. Symphony Technology Group invested in Celtra in November 2021. Mediaocean then agreed on November 21, 2024 to buy Innovid for $3.15 a share, an enterprise value of about $500 million, against a pre-deal market value of $240 million. The deal closed on February 13, 2025, placing two of Forrester's four 2020 leaders under one owner.
The vocabulary shifted alongside the ownership. Celtra now describes its product as creative automation and "creative enablement", Bannerflow calls itself a "creative intelligence" platform, and Forrester's 2020 category name avoided the CMP label altogether. Gartner still runs a peer-review market under the creative management platform label, listing 14 products as of October 2026, from Smartly.io and Bannerflow to Celtra Creative Automation and Mobvista's XMP.
Why the category matters
Automation has moved most media decisions into algorithms, which leaves creative as one of the few levers an advertiser fully controls. Platform systems such as Meta's Advantage+ and Google's Performance Max reward a large supply of assets to test. The demand is real, but the practice lags. A Perion and EMARKETER survey of 111 US marketers, published on April 15, 2026, found 89.2% considered creative important while only 3.6% said it was well understood and actively optimised. TripleLift's survey of 200 respondents, released on May 19, 2026, found 73% used artificial intelligence (AI) for optimisation but only 25% for creative production.
Independence is the other argument. A CMP lets a brand keep one asset library and one set of creative-level reports across channels, rather than rebuilding work inside each platform's tool. That case strengthens as platforms ship their own generators: Google launched Asset Studio on September 10, 2025, and more than one million advertisers used Meta's generative tools to create over 15 million ads in a single month, a figure reported in November 2025.
Where it falls short
Production volume does not equal delivery. Bannerflow's own data for January 1 to August 31, 2026, covering more than 300 brands and 2.33 million assets, showed that 78% of brands produced video but only 46% served it. Blended click-through rate across 155.1 billion impressions was 0.108%, and iGaming accounted for 76.1% of impressions, a skew that limits how far the figures generalise.
Performance claims are mostly self-reported. Smartly cited a 5.5x return on ad spend validated by PwC; Amazon reported an 8.4% lift in paid units from DCO in internal testing. Neither figure has been independently audited, and element-level attribution assumes components act independently, which they rarely do.
Platform dependence cuts both ways. Walled gardens can change APIs, formats or policies faster than third-party tools adapt, and their native generators cost advertisers nothing extra. Finally, the ad serving question remains unsettled: tools that only export tags leave measurement to someone else, while tools that serve ads compete directly with the ad servers their clients already pay for.
Not the same as
Consent management platform. The same acronym, CMP, names the tools that collect user consent and write the Transparency and Consent Framework (TCF) string. In privacy contexts that meaning dominates.
Dynamic creative optimisation. DCO assembles and selects a variant at the moment of serving, based on signals such as location or weather. Many CMPs include it, but a CMP can produce static variants with no real-time decisioning at all.
Digital asset management. A DAM stores and governs finished files. A CMP generates and distributes new ads from those files.
Ad server. An ad server delivers and counts impressions. Some CMPs serve ads; many hand that job to one. Forrester also used "CMP" in 2015 for content marketing platforms, an unrelated editorial category.
Recent developments
The category is being rebuilt around generative AI and agents. Adobe launched GenStudio for Performance Marketing on October 14, 2024, with brand checks on generated content and planned links to Meta, TikTok, Snap, Campaign Manager 360 and Microsoft Advertising. Smartly added a pre-flight scoring tool, Creative Predictive Potential, on November 18, 2025. Google added Gemini Omni video and one-click creative testing to Asset Studio at Google Marketing Live on May 20, 2026. On September 22, 2026, Typeface released Arc Graph, which converts brand guidelines into rules that carry into Claude and ChatGPT, with a person required to approve output before publication. The direction is clear, if unproven: brand governance, not production speed, is becoming the product.

Summary
Who: Vendors such as Celtra, Bannerflow, Smartly, Clinch, Jivox and Innovid with Flashtalking under Mediaocean, alongside Adobe and Typeface; used by brand studios, agencies, performance teams and publishers.
What: Software that produces, versions, approves, distributes and measures advertising creative from shared templates, data feeds and rules, often with dynamic optimisation and sometimes ad serving.
When: The label was in common use by 2017 as programmatic buying scaled; consolidation ran from Sizmek's 2019 collapse to Mediaocean's 2025 Innovid deal, and generative AI reshaped the category from 2024.
Where: Between design tools and buying platforms, feeding DSPs, ad servers, social ad managers, connected TV and digital out-of-home.
Why: Automated buying demands more creative variants than teams can build by hand, and a shared platform keeps brand control and creative-level measurement consistent across channels.
